I thought it was important while we're in DC to bring in the guy behind the markets.
This is the person who oversees as part of the organization, the CFTC. All these prediction
markets along with a lot more. I want to bring them in now. CFTC chair, Michael Selig. Michael,
welcome. You just started this. It was December. You got sworn in, right?
That's right. I've been in just over 100 days now.
Yeah. How has it been for 100 days?
It's been exciting. We, of course, have this prediction markets issue that has been
festering, lingering, and really taking off in the recent months. Of course, we oversea
over $500 trillion in ocean derivatives markets. There's a lot on our plate,
but we're really excited to be handling prediction markets, crypto, and all the
novel financial instruments that are now in our markets.
It really is interesting when you think about this because I think when you hear the CFTC,
you think of a lot of people think about something like prediction markets. It's been
on the news quite a bit. Very small slice as to what you do on a day-to-day basis.
I want to talk about just the entire perspective on where these things are going and what
the status of them is. This is a new thing to most people. Give us a quick overview as to
how the CFTC came under control of these markets and why all of a sudden they seem to be everywhere.
Well, the CFTC was established in the 70s and it was established to oversee our derivatives
markets. These markets until around the turn of around the 70s, 80s, 90s, really have been
agricultural markets first and foremost. Farmers, ranchers, producers use them to manage risk
in whether it's weather or their crop risk or the input cost, energy, that sort of thing.
Primarily catering to our commercial end users, but over the years we started to see that in
financial products. We saw interest rate derivatives, we saw currency derivatives, and
in the 90s we started to see political prediction markets start to emerge. We saw markets like
the Iowa electronic market that offered trading in potential election outcomes.
And the Democrats didn't like that a whole lot and so you started to see
pushback against many of the other exchanges that wanted to start to offer these on a broader,
more commercial basis. So the Iowa electronic market was for educational purposes. These
commercial markets like Colchee and Polymarket were actually in litigation with the CFTC
under the prior administration and Polymarket was driven offshore. Colchee was actually
won their litigation with the CFTC and was able to start offering these products.
And when I came into the seat just over 100 days ago, many of these novel prediction
market products were now out in trading and it's become a real interesting use case for
financial markets. Yeah, I mean, it's been fascinating to watch all of that happen. Of
course, the CFTC legal situation with Colchee, if I understand that very well, it ended in
like October 2024. So a few weeks before that election, that election, and in my view,
thankfully, Donald Trump won. Now we have, I think, a totally different approach
to these financial innovations. One that is not, I think, adversarial. Can you describe what you
think, what is your approach and what is the approach of the administration?
Well, prediction markets offer event contract derivatives. These are instruments that we
have the exclusive regulatory authority over. And although the prior administration really tried
to draw them offshore, we're setting up rules and regulations that accommodate these novel
markets because we believe that these markets have proven more reliable than the news media
in many cases. And they offer, unlike gambling and casinos and all of that, which are focused
on entertainment, they offer really positive externalities for our society because they
help check these fake stories in the news and the media. And they're a financial product
like anything else. Our statute was set up with a very broad definition of the term commodity.
So we are the commodity futures trading commission, but Congress rightfully anticipated
that you'd have derivatives on virtually anything and everything. They're financial
instruments that derive their value from another asset. And that asset could be
a sports event, a political event, the price of corn or grain or anything else.
And so we will affirmatively take that jurisdiction, we'll set up rules and regulations
for the market, but we will make sure that these markets are here in the United States
and they're here to stay. I'm curious as to how you view the utility, the public utility
of these markets, because first of all, a lot of times they're just fun. And I don't first
of all think that's the worst thing in the world that people actually enjoy their lives.
But the left, certainly Elizabeth Warren thinks that when I look at this, I was talking to
a friend of mine, he's in, I'm in Texas and he runs an air conditioning company.
And the difference in his bottom line between a month that is 90 degrees and 100 degrees on
average or 85 and 95 is massive. It could turn his entire year. And now these markets are
available for him to go in and he can hedge that temperature, right? Like he can now protect
his business against a potentially bad year. This is something he couldn't do before.
I see use cases like that. Is small business a big part of this picture?
How can this actually benefit the economy? We are seeing a real explosion of retail interests in
our derivatives markets and that's something we did not have before. Traditionally, these
markets, as I mentioned, were for commercial end users, farmers, ranchers, producers.
The financial institutions started to get involved and the contracts were expensive to
purchase. A typical derivatives contract requires you to put up significant money to
take a position. With these contracts, they're dollar contracts. Typically the outcome is going to
pay out based on an event. So it's 50, 50 odds. You pay 50 cents for your contract and you earn
a dollar. And that's really retail focus, but that works very well for, to your point, somebody
who just wants to purchase a little bit of additional insurance. And I will say there's many
of the farmers and ranchers out there that were not able to access hedging tools because
the big exchanges don't want to offer certain contracts and the prediction markets have been
really willing to offer a wide range of things because go figure in a free market, people
are willing to experiment and trade different products. Is this part of the reason the left
seems to be pushing back against them so much? It seems like they're totally fine when giant
corporations and everybody were able to hedge their risk, but when it comes down to some
regular person able to do that, they seem to be very upset about that. I do think that
could be part of it for sure. I mean, I think there is this concern that we're letting more
people participate in our financial markets. And for some reason the left thinks that's a bad
thing because they could lose their money or they're not responsible enough with their funds.
But I do think to the extent you're going to allow a big institution into the markets,
should allow everybody who wants to participate. And there's no reason that
big institutions can have better knowledge on the markets than an individual who maybe knows what
the weather is going to be because they're able to see what's happening in their local community.
So I do think it's important to allow more participation in our markets and make sure
we have rules and regulations around that activity. Can we talk a little bit about
some of the criticism? AOC has come out and she said, this is just the
casinoization of everything in our lives. We're now betting on everything.
When you hear criticism like that, how do you react to it?
I don't think this is turning our markets into casinos. And I think that criticism is really
unfair. What we're doing with these markets is setting clear guardrails and rules around
novel financial products. And these derivatives contracts are clearly within our regulatory
authority. They're no different than anything else that we trade in terms of you set up a
derivative. The underlying or the subject of that derivative can be virtually anything.
It can be a stock. It can be a corn. It could be grain. It could be sports or politics.
And so we can't discriminate. We're not merit based regulators where we say, okay,
it's acceptable for you to trade on agricultural products, but not on sports or politics.
So we want to set merit neutral rules and regulations and this protects investors. This
protects consumers. It protects people using the markets. It doesn't turn them into casinos.
These aren't designed for entertainment. They're designed for financial positions.
And it's not my job as a regulator to say you're investing in agricultural products or
stocks, and that's better for your portfolio and you'll be more successful there because
frankly, a lot of Americans don't have any specialized knowledge and they're going
to lose their money in those products. So I think that kind of criticism is very much
a merit based criticism. And that's really not what our regulatory agency was designed to do.
We're not a merit regulator. I love I think you use the term at one point merit policing,
which is like it's kind of shouldn't be what we're doing in these markets. We should let
people make their own decisions, at least in my view. Some people say though you're
acting very hands off here, right? You're like, hey, we know we're not merit policing
any of this. At the same time, you're allowing things like insider trading. I can't tell you
how many times, Michael, that I've heard that exact thing. People are able to just,
Mr. Beast is able to, his producers are able to go on there and make all this money
and steal other people's money because they know what's going to happen in a video.
Can you set the record straight here? Is insider trading legal?
Absolutely not. And that criticism is completely unfounded. Our statute expressly prohibits fraud,
manipulation, insider trading and abusive trading practices. And we police that.
But more than us policing it, the exchanges themselves are self regulatory organizations,
which means they have quasi government authority to police traders in their markets.
And we've seen exchanges take action against traders in the markets. They can find them,
they can kick them out of their markets. And then they refer those persons to us at the agency.
And we can take further action. We can refer to the DOJ to take criminal action as well.
So we are a cop on the beat and we are very much policing the markets. And of course,
it takes some time to build a case and bring an investigation. But people should not engage
in insider trading because they will be quickly dispensed with through the legal process.
The number one conversation I have with people about prediction markets is like,
well, what I'm doing wouldn't be insider trading, right? Like they're thinking like,
what if I know this? Can I do this? It is a somewhat difficult thing to figure out,
right? Because if you happen to just be really engaged in a process, you probably do know things
that maybe others don't. What is the line when it comes to insider trading?
So the insider trading case law articulates a pretty clear test. If you are a person that
obtained non-public information and you trade on that information in breach of a duty, whether it's
your employer or to, for example, you're a doctor, you've got a physician, privilege or confidentiality
with your patient, you're a lawyer, you trade on something that's confidential from your client.
Any of that, when you're breaching a duty and you trade on that information,
that's insider trading. It could be, for example, the doctor that's taken care of an
athlete and the athlete has an injury, the doctor knows that the athlete won't plan a game and so
they trade ahead of that. That's illegal. And we police that. And there's many such cases. You
can imagine lots of different stories of somebody had a duty to their employer and traded on it.
All of that's not allowed in our markets. And going beyond that, we also have standards
for contracts not being readily susceptible to manipulation. So even if something's not
insider tradeable or there's not this risk of insider trading, if the contract is easily
manipulable, so somebody could, for example, injure a player to win on a contract,
that sort of thing shouldn't be listed in our markets.
A lot of times, we hear these stories, the media loves stories, these outlier
kind of stories when it comes to prediction markets. Most of them are not even
occurring here in the United States. We hear these things about war, about death,
about assassination, all these markets. Are those markets legal here in the United States?
Those markets are also prohibited. Our statute includes a provision that states contracts on war,
assassination, terrorism, illegal activity, gaming, which is undefined, these are within
the agency's discretion to prohibit. And so we have not allowed and we can reject contracts.
We have not allowed any exchanges to list war, terrorism, assassination, and various other sorts
of contracts that are illegal offshore. We do not oversee the listing of contracts. So there are
some exchanges that list these things offshore and to the extent U.S. persons are accessing that
somehow, we have authority to the extent it's extraterritorial, but we don't oversee the
exchanges as their primary regulator. And that's where, I mean, all of these stories
seem to come from. Are these overseas exchanges that are not regulated by you?
That's right. You would not allow that to happen, right? That's not a thing that can occur.
That's right. Okay. Because I can't believe how many people don't understand that. One of the
big things I hear from people and including some conservatives and people that I agree with
on a lot of things, like we just can't let these things be the Wild West. It's not the Wild West,
right? You have regulatory authority over this and you're helping shape this as we go
with the attention, at least in my understanding, of allowing these markets and innovations to
flourish. Right. It's really an unfair criticism because if you think about, for example, our
regulation around food and drinks and all of that here in the United States, we allow certain things.
Other countries allow much more things, right? We have different standards. Some
countries have some more stringent standards. In the U.S., we have very stringent standards
around the listing of these contracts, but that's not to say that they can't be listed
offshore in a different exchange under different laws and regulations.
Right. I mean, I've eaten in some of these countries and did not work out well. I will tell
you. I'm glad we have some of those rules. Okay. Let me ask you another one. This is
the one I hear often actually from conservatives who say, we're federalists. We believe in
states' rights. We believe in the democracy laboratory that we've talked about since the
time of our founders. These states have gone out of their way to stop sports gambling.
You look at a state, Utah wants to say, hey, we don't want sports gambling. Why all of a sudden
can someone who wants to bet on sports now go on Cal State or Polymarket or one of these other
exchanges and bet on sports? Why can't they prevent these markets from appearing in their
states? Well, for over 100 years, we've had these futures markets, derivatives markets,
operating in parallel with the bucket shops, casinos, sports books, that sort of thing.
And they're different products and services. You have very different standards. And over the
years, we've had legal frameworks develop around derivatives and state frameworks develop around
gambling and casinos and bucket shops. And they've continued to exist in parallel.
The fact that you can have a bet on the price of virtually anything or you can have
a derivative instrument, there's different legal treatment. We have insurance contracts that also
look similar to derivatives contracts or securities that can look similar. So we've had parallel legal
frameworks for very different products. And the standards are different. Going back to the
example of food and beverage and all of that, one country can set different standards for
theirs. The United States sets their standards. Well, the states do have some authorities
that standards around gambling and entertainment and casinos. But when you get into financial
markets, when you get into structuring derivatives products, regardless of the underlying can be
sports, politics, corn grains, whatever it is, that falls within our exclusive regulatory
authority. So we have had a number of states bring legal actions, some criminal against
our exchanges for complying with federal law. And the federal law allows them to offer
derivatives contracts across state lines. You can't do entertainment, you can't offer
drinks, you can't do a house model where you kick people out of the casino if they win too much.
It's a different product and once for entertainment and that's great. And states have a lot of
authority. I believe in states' rights. I think it's really important for states to have the
authority to ban true gambling casinos and all of that. If they want to have that outside
their state and not allow it in their state, that's great. But the federal regime for financial
markets crosses state lines and we have to enforce our statute. It's interesting because,
as a conservative, as a person who is very much in favor of states being able to do what they
want to do in almost all cases, I am a massive opponent of the way the commerce clause has
been utilized over the years. I think it's been a catastrophe for a million different reasons.
But fundamentally, this is the type of thing it was designed for in the real world. It would be
wrong for us to go to someone in Utah and say, hey, you can't purchase Walmart stock. You
can't participate in the New York Stock Exchange or the NASDAQ because your state has decided to ban
you. Is that the right way to look at what's happening with these prediction markets?
That's the concern I have. If you think about a farmer, rancher, producer in the state of Utah,
if Utah is able to say you can't hedge your risk in your commercial business,
how is that any different than Utah saying, well, if there's this local sports team
or a local election and people can't hedge their risk related to that because
people are hedging that risk and people are speculating on it, and that's how we have markets.
So to me, anytime you start looking at, oh, well, this market is merit-based. We allow for this
and not allow for that. It really questions whether we truly are a free market economy and
we're going to allow for our markets to flourish here in the United States.
I like your approach to a lot of this. By far, my favorite thing about you is that
you're a Philadelphia Eagles fan. And it's interesting because I've talked to so many
people who bring up, there's no, yeah, sure, grain futures. Yeah, okay, I can see why you'd
need that weather. Maybe sure, but sports, the winner of American Idol, these things aren't
valuable to anyone. And my answer to this is, I will tell you, as a person who watches the
Eagles every single year, my day is good or bad, but based on the result. And there
is social value to me to hedge whether the Eagles are going to win or not. And I have actually
done that on these markets. It might make me a psychopath, but it is something that I do.
You're just nodding. That's making me, you understand as an Eagles fan.
You mentioned the merit policing thing. Do you don't have to judge it all,
whether there's a social value to this? Or is it something that you do see down the line
problems legally from maybe a different approach from Congress, where they say,
hey, we're going to sift out some of these sports contracts and reality show contracts?
Well, that's why we're engaging in rulemaking. So we do want all participants in the markets and
stakeholders and states to come engage with us to help us get the rules right. And there are
certain contracts that do raise concerns. I mentioned injury contracts earlier on. We don't
want to create perverse incentives for players to go injure other players. And there's also a
risk that that contract could easily be manipulated. So we are setting clear standards. And
that's critical in these markets. We can't have anything goes. But what's important
is that we set the gold standard here in the United States, because if we don't create a regulatory
infrastructure for these products here in the US, they just go offshore. We've seen that. And with
blockchain technology, you can offer this stuff on a global basis. And it's very hard to keep people
out of any sort of blockchain based application. You can't really censor the internet and
people's access to things. So we want to set a model that's a no brainer. If you think back
to the years of Napster and the illegal file sharing music, Spotify, iTunes, that all won out.
And we'll see the same in my view with prediction markets if we get it right here in the United
States. But if we create black markets and just push it offshore, it's not going to benefit
Americans. It'll just create, you know, offshore markets and people are going to get hurt.
Do we need new legislation on prediction markets or is the current sort of structure
enough? The commodity exchange act is one of the best pieces of legislation out there.
I mean, I'm biased because I implement it, but it has a lot of really interesting provisions that
are designed for fostering innovation. And actually one of our mandates as an agency is to
promote responsible innovation. But the statute has this very broad definition of commodity.
It includes everything except for onions and motion picture box office receipts
excluded for historical reasons and for lobbying by Mr. Dodd. But the statute is very broad.
So it covers a wide range of products and the definition of a swap post Dodd Frank prior to
Dodd Frank, we had very broad authority over options and futures, but swaps were included
under Dodd Frank. And so now we've even broader authority over different types of creative
financial instruments. So we really cover the waterfront when it comes to these products.
And we have a self certification process that allows the exchanges to quickly list products.
The SEC actually doesn't have this. So it's a it's a really helpful tool because in exchange
to come to market very quickly with new contracts and we have 24 hours to reject or approve.
Whereas if you're dealing with the SEC, you have to actually register your security and it takes
a very long time to come to market. You mentioned blockchain crypto. I know you've worked on
this before. Are we going to get new legislation? How important is it? I think it's very
important to future proof crypto markets here in the United States. We saw under the last
administration, Gary Gensler, who is the SEC chairman, regulate by enforcement and sue every
one of the major crypto companies in the United States. And the states are picking that up now.
So we're starting to see that again. And it's really important to have a federal framework where
you can opt into federal standards. And I think it's the same for prediction markets because
states can easily man things. And we want this technology here in the United States under a
federal framework similar with AI where if you have different standards across states,
the commerce class to your point was really designed to protect this stuff and make sure that
you don't have to move to California or move to Texas or move to Utah to be able to develop
your new technology or offer your markets. So I do think the legislation can help future
proof that make sure that future administrations can't take our crypto away from us. And I think
this is a very much American values based technology. Holding your own assets is really
critical. The Revolutionary War was fought very much for private property. And to have
a blockchain where no matter what you can't be censored and your assets can't be taken away
from you, I think that's really something we need to protect here in the United States.
There's a lot of opposition to it though. They don't like crypto. They don't
like prediction markets. There's a lot of pushback. Do we need on top of the crypto
legislation anything on top of the prediction markets to do the same thing to future proof
the industry? Well, unlike crypto, our statute's very clear that these are within our authority.
I think you're going to see pushback from the other side where there's an effort to try
to take away from us. So that I am concerned about on the Hill to the extent people want
undermine the CPC's authority. But of course, there's always things you can add to add more
clarity within our statute. And we're talking to folks on the Hill on a regular basis providing
technical assistance because we are subject matters experts when it comes to our statute.
But I do think there's a lot of parallel between the two technologies crypto and
prediction markets because one is really democratizing our information systems and
checking the news media and crypto is a check on the debanking and the financial institutions
that have centralized control over our assets and both should be protected here in the United
States if we want to really preserve our American values. Two more for you before I know you
have to go. Number one, would you I have a very long text chain battle going back and
forth with a friend of mine on the subject of whether avatar sucks or not the movie.
I looked for a market to try to go against him and say that he was they were going to
underperform the box office receipts. I was unable to find one. I had no idea until
I heard from you onions and box office receipts. Do we need to include in this
legislation to the clearance so I can just I can go out there and I can invest in my
onions because I like onion investment. Well, maybe the times come to revisit the Dodd
Frank language that the prohibited motion picture box office seats. And it's an
interesting history, right? Because cancer actually tried to launch a motion picture
box office sheets exchange and they were very far along. I don't know if it actually
ever launched. But then there was an effort from the motion picture box office association
to prohibit that. And lo and behold, we have a carve out in our statute.
This also demonstrates the fact that the framers of our statute thought very broadly
about what's a commodity. It's meant to include right beyond agricultural products,
things like movie receipts, sports, politics, all of it. And I think that really creates a lot
of space for novel financial instruments. But I think maybe the time has come we
would be visit motion picture box office receipts. And the onions one is crazy.
A couple of traders basically cornered the market on onions. Is that true? I read
they somehow were able to control 98 percent of all onions. Is that actually a real thing?
That's a real story. And it's interesting also because we've seen manipulation over the years
and in lots of different commodities and we police that. But there was a lot of lobbying,
I guess, to make sure that it never happens again with onions.
With onions. Okay. Last one for you. This is the most important one. The only thing I
really care about in this entire conversation, Michael, I'm sorry. I have a position on this
full disclosure. Will A.J. Brown be an eagle next season? I wish I could say yes. But I am
not feeling good about it. It's not looking good. Unfortunately, that is the position I have.
Unfortunately, Michael Sealeck, CFTC chair. I'm fascinated by all this. And I think,
you know, your approach here to protect these markets and make sure this innovation
lasts longer than just a fad. You know, turning this into something where people can actually
go in there and improve their lives through these markets. I think it's really,
really important. And thank you for your work on it. I appreciate that. Thank you.
All right. That's our interview with Michael Sealeck, a CFTC chair. He's the guy that
had the organization that oversees all prediction markets. As you mentioned,
with a couple of other things involved, $500 trillion. Just that and the $500 trillion.
I can't imagine how much of his time is spent actually dealing with

taking the time. One of the things I wanted to get to with him and we were able to cover
was, you know, this idea that, you know, you can just be an insider trading. You
can do insider trading. You can be an insider trader. You can go and you can,
you know, manipulate these markets. And this is just a casino.
All of these criticisms, you see kind of, I mean, it's mostly the left. Honestly,
there's some though on the right as well who are looking at this and just, you know,
frankly, don't understand. I was talking to a journalist last night and she was asking,
she's like, I don't, I kind of feel like there would be almost more pushback from people

Good luck. You might wind up in prison over it. And that's the case with

These things are illegal. If you're thinking about trying to do something like that,
do not do it. Stay away from it. Stay away from the line on it. I mean, I think, you know,
as conservatives, we're rule followers that away, right? Like we want to make sure that
there is order to our society. And these are new and people don't really understand what the

help you as a small business person. And that is really there. And of course,
also it can help you as an Eagles fan, which is, as I would say, probably more important to me
